statement: As described in an American Heart Association scientific statement and in narrative reviews (all figures second-hand; no primary study was read here, and the statement gives no search or appraisal method), studies of adults who use cannabis point in different directions on heart attack, stroke and other heart and blood-vessel disease, and the AHA writing group judged the evidence still inconclusive (Page et al., 2020). In the hour after use, the risk of a heart attack starting was 4.8 times that at other times in a case-crossover study of 3,882 people with a heart attack, an estimate printed without an interval that rests on few exposed people (9 had smoked cannabis within an hour of presenting with the heart attack, by the statement's account) (Mittleman et al., 2001, as relayed by Page et al., 2020, and Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015, calls it a quadrupling). Two surveys found more stroke: past-year use went with 3.3 times the rate of stroke or transient ischaemic attack, 2.3 (95% CI 1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related factors including tobacco smoking, with the excess confined to weekly or more frequent use (4.7, 2.1 to 10.7; adjustment not stated) (Hemachandra et al., 2016); and among adults aged 18 to 44, use went with an adjusted OR for stroke of 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), and 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) with use on more than 10 days a month (Parekh et al., 2020; adjustment set not stated). Health-record and hospital databases report more heart attacks where cannabis use is recorded, for example 1.37% against 0.54% over 3 years (about 14 against 5 in 1,000, editors' conversion; RR 2.53, adjustment not stated; Chami & Kim, 2019), but the statement warns that samples of hospitalised patients carry a high probability of selection bias. Against these, in the CARDIA cohort (5,113 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start, followed for more than 25 years) cumulative lifetime and recent use were not associated with new cardiovascular disease, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, coronary heart disease or cardiac death (Reis et al., 2017; no estimates printed). After a heart attack the findings run both ways: long-term mortality was 29% higher in people who used cannabis but not significantly (95% CI 0.81 to 2.05; adjustment not stated; Frost et al., 2013), while among 2,097 young adults treated for a heart attack at two academic hospitals, all-cause and cardiovascular mortality were higher (adjusted HR 1.99 and 2.22; no intervals printed) in people who used cocaine and marijuana, as the statement's table words it, which does not isolate cannabis (DeFilippis et al., 2018). Laboratory studies show dose-related rises in heart rate, to which healthy young adults quickly become tolerant, and angina brought on by smoking cannabis in people with heart disease (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; the angina finding also in Page et al., 2020). The statement names short-term, observational and retrospective designs, poorly measured exposure, recall bias, low-risk cohorts and confounding by tobacco as the main weaknesses, and judges the evidence for people with cardiac risk factors insufficient; Hall (2015) concludes that cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of heart attack. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does cannabis cause heart attacks or strokes? This has not been shown. In one study, a heart attack was more likely to start in the hour after using cannabis, and two surveys found more strokes, mostly in people who used cannabis every week or more. Hospital records also show more heart attacks in people who use cannabis, but these records are hard to interpret. A study that followed young adults for over 25 years found no link with heart disease or stroke. In lab studies, cannabis raised heart rate and brought on chest pain (angina) in people with heart disease. The American Heart Association called the evidence inconclusive. These figures come from reviews, not from the studies themselves, and the studies could not fully separate cannabis from tobacco. See the contested question.
population: Adults in studies relayed by an American Heart Association statement and narrative reviews: people with a heart attack (a US case-crossover study and its follow-up), population survey samples, US hospital and health-record databases, and young US adults in the CARDIA cohort
exposure: Cannabis use as each relayed study recorded it: use in the hour before a heart attack (case-crossover); past-year use, weekly or more, or more than 10 days a month (stroke surveys); recorded use or diagnosis codes (hospital databases); cumulative lifetime and recent use (CARDIA)
comparator: The same people at other times (case-crossover); people without reported or recorded use in the same survey, cohort or database; placebo in laboratory studies
outcome: Onset of heart attack; stroke or transient ischaemic attack; heart attacks in hospital records; new cardiovascular disease, coronary heart disease and cardiac death; death after a heart attack; heart rate and angina
magnitude: All second-hand. Case-crossover (Mittleman et al. 2001, 3,882 people with a heart attack): onset 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after use (no interval; 9 people had smoked cannabis within 1 hour of presentation); follow-up of 1,913: mortality over 3.8 years 2.5 times with use less than weekly and 4.2 times with use more than weekly (as relayed by Hall & Degenhardt 2009, without intervals; the AHA statement says many mortality findings of these smaller follow-up studies did not reach statistical significance). Stroke: Hemachandra et al. 2016, past-year use, rate ratio 3.3 (1.8 to 6.3) before and 2.3 (1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco, 4.7 (2.1 to 10.7) for weekly or more frequent use; Parekh et al. 2020, adults aged 18 to 44, adjusted OR 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) for use on more than 10 days a month, and, for that frequent use together with combustible-cigarette use, 3.12 (1.40 to 6.97), and with e-cigarette use, 2.63 (1.07 to 6.46), each against people who did not use cannabis. Databases: Chami & Kim 2019, 3-year heart-attack incidence 1.37% vs 0.54% (about 14 vs 5 in 1,000, editors' conversion), RR 2.53 (2.45 to 2.61); Desai et al. 2019, heart-attack admissions of young adults 0.23% vs 0.14%. CARDIA (Reis et al. 2017, 5,113 adults, over 25 years): no association, no estimates printed. After a heart attack: Frost et al. 2013, mortality 29% higher, 95% CI 0.81 to 2.05, P = 0.28; DeFilippis et al. 2018, 2,097 young adults, adjusted HR 1.99 (all-cause) and 2.22 (cardiovascular) among people who used cocaine and marijuana, no intervals; Johnson-Sasso et al. 2018, mortality OR 0.79 (short-term outcomes by the reference title; no interval or adjustment printed). Laboratory: exercise time to angina 48% shorter after one cannabis cigarette than after placebo.

evidence.extracted: The AHA writing group's overall judgment: evidence on cannabis use and adverse cardiovascular outcomes is still inconclusive, with an urgent need for carefully designed prospective short- and long-term studies and, ideally, controlled trials of different forms and routes; for people with cardiac risk factors it judges the present evidence for a link insufficient, citing limited longitudinal data and recall bias in cross-sectional studies.
evidence.quote: evidence is still inconclusive for cannabis use and adverse cardiovascular outcomes

evidence.page: pp. e1–e2, e19–e20 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Abstract; introduction (unheaded), 1st paragraph (starts p. e1); Article Information, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (p. e19); Reviewer Disclosures table (p. e20)
evidence.extracted: Method as stated: the writing group describes the statement as a critical review of medicinal and recreational cannabis from clinical, policy and public-health perspectives, focused on cardiovascular health; no search strategy, databases, dates, inclusion criteria, appraisal method or grading system is described; it was approved by two AHA committees and peer-reviewed through the AHA by four named reviewers.

evidence.page: pp. e9–e10 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 2nd paragraph (p. e9), 3rd paragraph (starts p. e9) and 4th paragraph (p. e10)
evidence.extracted: Weaknesses the statement names: most data are short-term, observational and retrospective, with poorly determined exposure, recall bias, minimal exposure without dose or product standardisation and typically low-risk cohorts; epidemiological studies may be confounded by access to health care and other behaviours such as tobacco use; rising THC content may make earlier studies less relevant; few data come from rigorous prospective cohorts; signals for adverse cardiac outcomes come mostly from hospitalised patients, where a high probability of selection bias makes cannabis as a cause of hospitalisation uncertain; and concomitant tobacco and other drug use is inadequately handled in data collection and statistical adjustment.

evidence.page: pp. e12, e17 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Table 3, row Mittleman et al (p. e12); Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, paragraph (p. e17)
evidence.extracted: As relayed (Mittleman et al., case-crossover design, 3882 patients with acute myocardial infarction): risk of infarction onset 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after cannabis use (no interval printed); 3% of the patients had smoked cannabis in the prior year, 37 within 24 hours and 9 within 1 hour of presentation; people who used cannabis were more likely to be men, cigarette smokers and obese.

evidence.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 7th paragraph (left column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized: evidence exists to support adverse cardiovascular effects; cannabis and THC raise heart rate in a dose-dependent way, marginally affecting healthy young adults, who quickly develop tolerance, with concern for adults with cardiovascular disease. In a case-crossover study of 3882 people who had had a myocardial infarction, cannabis use increased the risk of infarction 4.8 times in the hour after use; a prospective study of 1913 of them found a dose–response relation with mortality over 3.8 years, risk 2.5 times with use less than once a week and 4.2 times with use more than once a week; laboratory studies show that smoking cannabis provokes angina in people with heart disease.

evidence.locator: Cardiovascular effects, 1st paragraph (begins p. 9, continues p. 10) and 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 10); Table 1 and WHAT HAVE WE LEARNED IN 20 YEARS? › Physical health outcomes (p. 12)
evidence.extracted: As summarized: in 1993 laboratory studies showed dose-related rises in heart rate with rapid tolerance in healthy young adults, and angina in older adults with cardiovascular disease; the evidence has not increased a great deal since, but is called consistent with adverse cardiovascular effects in middle-aged and older adults. The same case-crossover study of 3882 people is said to show the risk of infarction quadrupled in the hour after smoking, and its follow-up of 1913 a dose–response with mortality over 3.8 years; a French series of 200 cannabis-related hospitalisations (Toulouse area, January 2004 to December 2007) included several infarctions and a fatal stroke in young adults with recent use and no other known risk factors. Table 1 gives the strength of effect for cardiovascular disease as 3–4-fold for myocardial infarction (its symbols are undefined), and the conclusions say cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of myocardial infarction.

evidence.page: pp. e10, e12, e14, e17, e21 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 5th paragraph (p. e10); Table 3, row Hemachandra et al (p. e12); Considerations in Special Populations › Young Adults, paragraph (p. e14); Patients With Cardiac Risk Factors, paragraph (p. e17); References, ref 68 (p. e21)
evidence.extracted: As relayed: in a population survey (PATH Through Life, age cohorts 20–24, 40–44 and 60–64, surveyed 1999–2002; Hemachandra et al.), people with past-year cannabis use (n = 1043) had 3.3 times the rate of stroke or transient ischaemic attack (95% CI 1.8 to 6.3), a rate ratio of 2.3 (1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco smoking, with stroke or TIA in people using weekly or more often (4.7, 2.1 to 10.7) and no elevation at lower frequency. In the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, among adults aged 18 to 44 (Parekh et al., 2020, ref 68), the adjusted OR for stroke was 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10) for people who used marijuana against those who did not, 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) for use on more than 10 days a month, 3.12 (1.40 to 6.97) for frequent use with combustible cigarettes and 2.63 (1.07 to 6.46) with e-cigarettes; adjustment sets not stated. The text and Table 3 give different cohort sizes (study card reporting issue).

evidence.page: p. e11 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Table 3, rows Chami and Kim and Desai et al (ref 33)
evidence.extracted: As relayed: in an aggregate multi-institutional health-record database (Explorys, 2011–2016), people with a history of cannabis use (labelled the cannabis abuse group) had, against more than 10 million controls, a 3-year cumulative incidence of acute myocardial infarction of 1.37% against 0.54% (RR 2.53, 95% CI 2.45 to 2.61; adjustment not stated). In the National Inpatient Sample 2007–2014 (more than 52 million hospitalisations; cannabis use without other substance use), admissions for myocardial infarction in young adults were 0.23% against 0.14%, arrhythmia and stroke were more frequent and venous thromboembolism less frequent in people who used cannabis (editors' conversion of the first pair: about 14 and 5 in 1,000).

evidence.page: p. e12 of the online-first PDF
evidence.extracted: As relayed: a systematic review of 85 studies, case reports and case series (Richards et al.) found that 28 of 33 studies evaluated suggested an increased risk of both acute coronary syndrome and chronic cardiovascular disease from cannabis use; of 51 case reports or series with 62 people, 21 (34%) had cardiomyopathy and 14 deaths (23%) were attributed to acute coronary syndrome.

evidence.page: pp. e9–e10, e12 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 3rd paragraph (starts p. e9); Table 3, row Reis et al (p. e12)
evidence.extracted: As relayed (Reis et al., CARDIA, 1985–1986 baseline): in 5113 adults aged 18 to 30 at baseline, followed for more than 25 years, cumulative lifetime and recent cannabis use showed no association with incident cardiovascular disease, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, coronary heart disease or cardiac mortality; no estimates, intervals or adjustment set are printed. The text cites this finding to another CARDIA paper, while Table 3 and the reference list attribute it to Reis et al. (study card reporting issue).

evidence.page: pp. e10–e11 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 4th paragraph (p. e10); Table 3, row Auer et al (p. e11)
evidence.extracted: As relayed (Auer et al., CARDIA, 3498 participants): among people who had ever smoked tobacco, marijuana exposure was associated with higher abdominal aortic and coronary artery calcium scores, and among people who had never smoked tobacco it was not; no numbers are printed.

evidence.page: pp. e11–e12 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Table 3, rows Frost et al (p. e11) and Johnson-Sasso et al (p. e12)
evidence.extracted: As relayed: among 3886 people who had had a myocardial infarction (Frost et al., Determinants of MI Onset Study, National Death Index), mortality was 29% higher in people who used cannabis than in those who did not, not statistically significant (95% CI 0.81 to 2.05; P = 0.28). In hospital records from 8 states, 1994–2013, of more than 1.2 million patients with myocardial infarction, 3854 (about 0.3%) reported cannabis use; the composite primary outcome (death, intra-aortic balloon pump, mechanical ventilation, cardiac arrest, shock) was not associated with cannabis use and mortality was lower (OR 0.79, no interval).

evidence.page: p. e17 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, paragraph
evidence.extracted: As relayed: in people with chronic stable angina, smoking a single cannabis cigarette shortened exercise time to angina by 48% compared with placebo (sample size not given); the statement reasons that because cannabis raises myocardial oxygen demand and lowers supply, people with ischaemic heart disease could have more angina, particularly when cannabis is smoked.

evidence.page: p. e10 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 6th paragraph
evidence.extracted: As relayed: smoking cannabis has been associated, controversially, with a cannabis arteritis resembling thromboangiitis obliterans, and more than 20% of lower-limb arteriopathy in young adults may be caused by it, an estimate the statement says may be confounded because 97% of people who smoke cannabis also smoke tobacco.

evidence.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF CANCER AND OTHER EFFECTS ON HEALTH, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: As summarized: marijuana use has been associated with vascular conditions that raise the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke and transient ischaemic attack during intoxication (citing a review), with direct effects on CB1 receptors in arteries and indirect effects on vasoactive compounds offered as explanations (citing a review and, by its title, a case report).
evidence.located_by: AI reader 210 (claim writer), from AI reader 188's study card
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC4827335 (NIH author manuscript of N Engl J Med 2014;370(23):2219-2227)

evidence.page: pp. e11, e17, e21–e22 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Table 3, row DeFilippis et al (p. e11); Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, paragraph (p. e17); References, refs 32, 37 and 87 (pp. e21–e22)
evidence.extracted: As relayed: in 2097 young adults with myocardial infarction at 2 academic hospitals, 2000–2016 (DeFilippis et al., 2018, ref 32, titled as a study of cocaine and marijuana use), adjusted HRs of 1.99 for all-cause and 2.22 for cardiovascular mortality are given among people who used cocaine and marijuana (no intervals; whether the exposures were combined is not said); the text says cannabis use is present in 6% of patients aged 50 or younger presenting with AMI and is associated with worse all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. The text adds that smaller studies (refs 37 and 87: Frost et al., 2013, on long-term mortality among survivors of myocardial infarction, and Mukamal et al., 2008, an exploratory prospective study of mortality after myocardial infarction, by their titles) have shown a signal toward higher mortality in coronary artery disease with cannabis use, although many of these findings failed to reach statistical significance.

risk_of_bias.note: Not appraisable at the level of the primary studies: the AHA statement gives no search, selection rule or appraisal (card sc_page_2020: overall high) and the narrative reviews are unsystematic (cards sc_hall_2009, sc_hall_2015, sc_volkow_2014). The relayed studies are mostly hospital databases with selection bias, surveys with self-reported use and case reports, with adjustment unstated in most and tobacco use inadequately handled, as the statement itself says.

inconsistency.note: The long prospective cohort found no association while the case-crossover, survey and database studies did; outcomes after a heart attack run both ways (non-significantly higher long-term mortality, lower in-hospital mortality); one case-crossover estimate is given as 4.8 times, a quadrupling and 3–4-fold by the reviews.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: every figure is a review's account of studies not read here (METHODS §6.3), and several rows of the statement's table cannot be right as printed (card sc_page_2020, reporting issues).

imprecision.note: The trigger estimate rests on few exposed people (9 had used within an hour of presentation, by the statement's account) and has no interval; stroke intervals are wide (2.1 to 10.7; 1.08 to 3.10); the CARDIA null is printed without estimates, so its precision is unknown; the mortality hazard ratios after a heart attack have no intervals.

large_effect.note: The 4.8-fold trigger estimate rests on few exposed people, without an interval or adjustment; no upgrade.

dose_response.note: Gradients by frequency (mortality after a heart attack; stroke with weekly or more frequent use) come second-hand from single studies without stated adjustment, and the AHA statement says many of the mortality findings did not reach statistical significance; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence seen only through reviews starts low and is downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision: very low, the floor. Overlapping sources are counted once: Hall & Degenhardt (2009), Hall (2015) and the AHA statement relay the same case-crossover study, and its mortality follow-ups (the 1,913-person study and Frost et al., 2013) come from the same onset study, so the trigger, the mortality gradient and the non-significant long-term mortality are not independent; the statement's inpatient analyses largely share one database. Contested because credible designs disagree (the long cohort against the trigger, survey and database studies; after a heart attack, a non-significant excess, a lower short-term mortality and a higher mortality in people who used cocaine and marijuana) and the reviews read the same evidence differently (still inconclusive for the AHA; probable for middle-aged adults in Hall, 2015). The claim rests only on second-hand sources (a professional statement without a stated search, and narrative reviews), so it stays at draft and says so (METHODS §6.3).

debate.question: Does using cannabis raise the risk of heart attack, stroke or other heart and blood-vessel disease?
debate.evidence_yes: In a case-crossover study of 3,882 people with a heart attack, the risk of onset in the 60 minutes after cannabis use was 4.8 times baseline; 37 had smoked cannabis within 24 hours and 9 within 1 hour of presentation (Mittleman et al., as relayed by Page et al., 2020, and Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), and in a follow-up of 1,913 of them mortality over 3.8 years rose with frequency of use, 2.5 times with use less than weekly and 4.2 times with use more than weekly (as relayed by Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, without intervals; the AHA statement says many mortality findings of these smaller follow-up studies did not reach statistical significance). Among 2,097 young adults treated for a heart attack at two academic hospitals, adjusted hazard ratios for all-cause and cardiovascular death were 1.99 and 2.22 among people who used cocaine and marijuana, as the statement's table words it (DeFilippis et al., 2018, as relayed by Page et al., 2020). In a population survey, past-year use went with 3.3 times the rate of stroke or transient ischaemic attack and a rate ratio of 2.3 (1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment that included tobacco, the excess lying in weekly or more frequent use (4.7, 2.1 to 10.7); in a US survey of adults aged 18 to 44 the adjusted OR for stroke was 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), and 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) with use on more than 10 days a month (Parekh et al., 2020; both as relayed by Page et al., 2020). A health-record database found a 3-year incidence of heart attack of 1.37% against 0.54% (RR 2.53, 2.45 to 2.61), an inpatient database found heart-attack admissions of young adults of 0.23% against 0.14% among people using cannabis without other substances, and a systematic review of studies and case reports found that 28 of 33 studies suggested a higher risk of both acute coronary syndrome and chronic cardiovascular disease (all as relayed by Page et al., 2020). Laboratory studies show dose-related rises in heart rate and angina brought on by smoking cannabis in people with heart disease, exercise time to angina falling by 48% against placebo in one. Hall (2015) reads the evidence as consistent with adverse cardiovascular effects in middle-aged and older adults, adds a French series of cannabis-related hospitalisations that included heart attacks and a fatal stroke in young adults with no other known risk factors, and concludes that cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of heart attack; Volkow et al. (2014) describe use as associated with vascular conditions that raise the risk of heart attack, stroke and transient ischaemic attack during intoxication.
debate.evidence_no: In the CARDIA cohort, 5,113 adults aged 18 to 30 at the 1985–1986 baseline and followed for more than 25 years, cumulative lifetime and recent use were not associated with new cardiovascular disease, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, coronary heart disease or cardiac death (Reis et al., as relayed by Page et al., 2020), and in the same cohort higher aortic and coronary calcium went with cannabis only in people who had ever smoked tobacco (Auer et al., 3,498 participants). After a heart attack, long-term mortality was 29% higher in people who used cannabis but not significantly (95% CI 0.81 to 2.05; 3,886 patients; Frost et al.), and in hospital records of more than 1.2 million heart-attack patients a composite outcome (death, balloon pump, ventilation, cardiac arrest or shock) was not associated with cannabis use and mortality was lower (OR 0.79, no interval; short-term outcomes by the reference title; Johnson-Sasso et al.). The AHA statement warns that studies restricted to hospitalised patients carry a high probability of selection bias, so cannabis as a cause of hospitalisation is uncertain; that most data are short-term, observational and retrospective, with poorly determined exposure, recall bias and low-risk cohorts; and that tobacco and other drug use are inadequately handled in data collection and adjustment; citing a review of cannabis arteritis, it gives 97% as the share of people who smoke cannabis who also smoke tobacco. The 4.8-fold trigger estimate has no printed interval and rests on few exposed people, the 4.7 estimate for weekly use has no stated adjustment, the higher mortality after a heart attack in young adults is given for cocaine and marijuana use together, and the database estimates are crude or silent on adjustment (Page et al., 2020). The AHA writing group judges the evidence still inconclusive overall and insufficient for people with cardiac risk factors.
debate.neither_can_show: Whether cannabis itself causes any of these events: none of the relayed studies convincingly separates cannabis from tobacco, which most people who smoke cannabis also use, or from other drugs, and none is a sibling comparison or a genetically informed design. The case-crossover design removes stable differences between people, but it concerns the minutes to hours after use and rests on few exposed people and on their recall of timing, while CARDIA concerns decades of use in young adults with few events, so the two results need not conflict. Whether results from smoked cannabis apply to eating or vaping it, and whether older studies apply to today's stronger products, which the statement itself questions. How large any risk is for a given person: no source gives absolute rates by age and baseline risk. All figures here are second-hand, and several rows of the statement's own table cannot be right as printed (card sc_page_2020).
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). From second-hand sources only: the clearest signal is short-lived, a higher chance of a heart attack starting in the hour after use, from one case-crossover study with few exposed people, together with laboratory evidence that cannabis raises heart rate and can bring on angina in people with heart disease. Signals for stroke come from two surveys and lie mainly in frequent use; the hospital-database associations are hard to read because of selection bias, unstated adjustment and tobacco. The one long cohort of young adults found no association with new heart disease or stroke over 25 years, which fits a short-lived trigger as well as no effect, because such a cohort has few events. After a heart attack the relayed findings run both ways, and the one higher-mortality estimate does not separate cannabis from cocaine. The AHA judges the evidence inconclusive and, for people with cardiac risk factors, insufficient, and the editors agree that no long-term risk figure can be given from these sources. The primary studies themselves have not been read for this page.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Large prospective cohorts, or a pooled analysis of existing ones, with repeated measures of how often, by which route and how strong the cannabis used is, and of tobacco, analysed separately in people who have never smoked tobacco, with confirmed heart attacks, strokes, rhythm problems and cardiac deaths and absolute risks by age and baseline risk; case-crossover studies with objectively timed use; sibling or genetically informed designs; and a systematic review with a stated search and risk-of-bias appraisal to bring them together (the AHA statement calls for carefully designed prospective short- and long-term studies).
